t: Fire triangle: heat, oxygen, fuel; PASS.

nota.t: Personal protective equipment (PPE) protects lab users from chemicals, heat, broken glass and microorganisms: lab coat, gloves, goggles, face mask and closed shoes. A fume chamber is used for volatile or toxic substances; a laminar flow cabinet for aseptic microbiology work. Biosafety cabinets follow levels BSL 1 to 4.

t: A fume chamber draws toxic gas out

nota.t: Lab waste is separated by type: chemical waste (labelled containers, never down the sink), biological waste (autoclaved before disposal), broken glass (special bin) and radioactive material (lead containers). Scheduled-waste regulations control the disposal of hazardous waste.

Fire needs the three parts of the fire triangle: fuel, oxygen and heat. Removing any one puts it out. Fire classes: A (solids), B (flammable liquids), C (gases), D (metals), E (electrical), F (cooking oil). Extinguishers: water (A), foam (A, B), dry powder (A, B, C, E), CO₂ (B, E). Use P.A.S.S.: Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep.

t: Aim at the base of the fire
DRSABC; 30 compressions : 2 breaths; 100–120 per minute; 5–6 cm.

nota.t: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) keeps blood and oxygen flowing when a person's heart and breathing have stopped. Check DRSABC: Danger, Response, Shout for help, Airway, Breathing, Circulation. Give 30 chest compressions (5–6 cm deep, 100–120 per minute) then 2 rescue breaths, and repeat until help arrives.

t: Do not move a spinal-injury victim

nota.t: The Heimlich manoeuvre clears a blocked airway in a choking person. Stand behind them, make a fist above the navel, grasp it with the other hand and give quick inward-upward thrusts until the object comes out. For a baby, use 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts.

t: Place the heel of the hand on the chest centre

topik.nama: 3. Techniques of Measuring Body Health Parameters

t: Temperature 36.5–37.5 °C; pulse 60–100 per minute; blood pressure ~120/80 mmHg.

nota.t: Normal body temperature is about 36.5 °C to 37.5 °C, controlled by the hypothalamus through homeostasis. It is measured with a digital, infrared or clinical thermometer at the mouth, armpit, ear or forehead. Fever (> 37.5 °C) signals infection; hypothermia (< 35 °C) is dangerous.

Pulse rate is the number of heartbeats per minute, felt at the wrist (radial pulse) or neck (carotid pulse). Normal adult rate: 60–100 beats per minute. It rises with exercise, fever or stress and is lower in athletes.
Example: 18 beats in 15 seconds → 18 × 4 = 72 beats per minute.

Blood pressure is the pressure of blood on artery walls, written systolic/diastolic in mmHg. Normal is about 120/80 mmHg. Systolic is the pressure when the ventricles contract; diastolic when the heart relaxes. Hypertension (≥ 140/90) raises the risk of stroke and heart disease. It is measured with a sphygmomanometer.
Body Mass Index BMI = mass (kg) ÷ [height (m)]². Categories: < 18.5 underweight; 18.5–24.9 normal; 25–29.9 overweight; ≥ 30 obese. BMI is a rough guide and does not tell muscle from fat.

t: Energy, waste, agriculture, transport and daily life.

nota.t: Environmental sustainability means meeting present needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs. The 5R principle: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Rethink, Repair. The UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) support this.

Green technology in energy uses renewable sources (solar, wind, hydro, biomass) and improves energy efficiency, for example solar PV panels, LED lights, green buildings and feed-in tariffs (FiT). This cuts greenhouse gas emissions.
Green waste and waste-water management: separating waste at source, composting, sanitary landfills, waste-to-energy and sewage treatment plants that produce biogas and treated water for reuse.

Green technology in agriculture and forestry: fertigation, hydroponics, aeroponics, biological pest control, organic fertiliser, precision farming with drones and sensors, and reforestation with selective logging.
Green transport reduces fossil fuel burning: electric and hybrid vehicles, biodiesel (B10, B20), public transport such as MRT and LRT, and cycling and walking.
Green technology in daily life: saving energy and water, buying eco-labelled products, cutting single-use plastic and supporting green buildings. Everyone helps reduce their carbon footprint.

Tt × Tt → 3 : 1. Gene and chromosome mutations.

nota.t: Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid (2n) daughter cells for growth, repair and asexual reproduction. Stages: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, then cytokinesis. Meiosis produces four genetically different haploid (n) daughter cells to form gametes; crossing over occurs.

Mendelian inheritance: each trait is controlled by a pair of alleles. A dominant allele (T) masks a recessive allele (t). Genotype is the allele combination (TT, Tt, tt); phenotype is the visible trait. A monohybrid cross Tt × Tt gives a 3 : 1 phenotype ratio.

A mutation is a random change in genetic material. Gene mutation changes the DNA base sequence (e.g. sickle-cell anaemia, albinism); chromosome mutation changes chromosome structure or number (e.g. Down syndrome, 47 chromosomes). Mutagens include UV rays, X-rays and chemicals such as asbestos.

Genetic engineering moves genes from one organism to another to make genetically modified organisms (GMOs). Examples: bacteria making human insulin, pest-resistant crops, golden rice rich in vitamin A. Gene therapy treats genetic disease. Issues: food safety, biodiversity and ethics.

Variation is the difference in traits between individuals of a species. Continuous variation shows a graded range (height, mass) with a normal distribution; discontinuous variation has clear categories (blood group, tongue rolling). Causes: genes and environment.
6.1 Support, Movement and Growth in Animals

Animals are supported by an exoskeleton (insects, crabs), an endoskeleton (vertebrates) or a hydrostatic skeleton (earthworms, using fluid pressure). Insects grow by ecdysis (moulting), giving a step-shaped growth curve.

The human skeleton (206 bones) supports, protects organs and allows movement. Joints: hinge (elbow, knee), ball-and-socket (shoulder, hip), gliding and pivot. Muscles work in antagonistic pairs: the biceps contracts and triceps relaxes to bend the arm. Human growth follows a sigmoid curve. Osteoporosis weakens bones.
6.3 Support, Growth and Stability in Plants

Plants are supported by turgor pressure in cells, woody tissue (xylem, lignin) and special structures: buttress roots, prop roots (maize), tendrils (cucumber), thorns and climbing stems. Primary growth lengthens shoots and roots; secondary growth thickens stems (annual rings).

t: Pituitary, thyroid, pancreas, adrenal, ovary, testis.

nota.t: The endocrine system has ductless glands that secrete hormones straight into the blood. Pituitary (growth hormone, the 'master gland'), thyroid (thyroxine, metabolism), adrenal (adrenaline, 'fight or flight'), pancreas (insulin and glucagon, blood glucose), ovaries (oestrogen) and testes (testosterone).

Body coordination is disrupted by hormone imbalance (diabetes mellitus from too little insulin, gigantism and dwarfism from growth hormone, goitre from lack of iodine) or by drug and alcohol abuse, which affect the nervous system and cause addiction and health problems.

A healthy mind means mental, emotional and social well-being: coping with stress, working productively and contributing to society. Harmful factors: stress, drugs, alcohol and lack of sleep. Keep healthy with exercise, enough sleep, a balanced diet, talking about problems and getting counselling.

t: Group by valence electrons; period by number of shells.

nota.t: Matter is made of tiny particles (atoms, molecules, ions) in constant motion. In solids they are closely packed and vibrate; in liquids close but free to move; in gases far apart and moving fast and randomly. Changes of state: melting, boiling, condensation, freezing, sublimation.

v.c: Particles in the three states of matter

nota.t: The Modern Periodic Table arranges 118 elements by increasing proton number. Vertical columns are groups (1–18): elements in a group share the same number of valence electrons and similar chemistry. Horizontal rows are periods (1–7): elements in a period have the same number of occupied shells. Metals on the left, non-metals on the right, noble gases in Group 18.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so different nucleon numbers. Examples: hydrogen-1, deuterium (²H), tritium (³H); carbon-12 and carbon-14. Uses: carbon-14 for dating, cobalt-60 for radiotherapy, iodine-131 for thyroid treatment, sodium-24 for detecting pipe leaks.

t: Alloys are harder; glass and ceramics; natural and synthetic polymers.

nota.t: An alloy is a metal mixed with other elements to make it stronger, harder and more corrosion-resistant. Foreign atoms of a different size stop the layers of pure metal atoms from sliding. Examples: steel (iron + carbon), stainless steel (iron + chromium + nickel), bronze (copper + tin), brass (copper + zinc), duralumin (aluminium + copper + magnesium).

Glass is made from molten silica (SiO₂). Types: fused silica glass (withstands high heat), soda-lime glass (cheap, windows and bottles), borosilicate glass (Pyrex, lab ware), lead crystal glass (sparkling). Ceramics are made by heating clay to high temperatures: hard, heat-resistant and electrical insulators; advanced ceramics are used in engines and electronic chips.

A polymer is a large molecule made of many monomers joined by polymerisation. Natural polymers: starch, protein, natural rubber, cellulose. Synthetic polymers: polythene (plastic bags), PVC (pipes), nylon, polystyrene. Non-biodegradable plastics cause pollution; tackle this with recycling and biodegradable plastics.

t: Free radicals and antioxidants; safe health products.

nota.t: Traditional medicine uses natural materials and inherited practices (herbs such as tongkat ali and turmeric; acupuncture). Modern medicine is based on science and clinical trials (antibiotics, vaccines, surgery). Complementary medicine supports modern treatment (massage, homeopathy, ayurveda). All treatments must be safe and registered.

A free radical is an atom or molecule with an unpaired electron, making it very reactive. It damages cells, DNA and proteins by stealing electrons, leading to ageing, cancer and heart disease. Sources: cigarette smoke, UV rays, air pollution and fried food.

v.c: A free radical with an unpaired electron

nota.t: An antioxidant gives an electron to a free radical to neutralise it without becoming harmful itself. Examples: vitamin C (citrus fruit), vitamin E (nuts), beta-carotene (carrots), flavonoids (green tea). Antioxidants are also used as food preservatives.

Health products include medicines, supplements, herbal products and cosmetics. Check the label: MAL registration number (Ministry of Health), security hologram, expiry date and ingredients. Avoid products with banned substances such as mercury or hidden steroids.

t: a = (v − u)/t; s–t gradient = velocity; v–t area = displacement.

nota.t: Linear motion is motion in a straight line. Distance is the path length (scalar); displacement is distance in a given direction (vector). Speed = distance/time; velocity = displacement/time. Acceleration a = (v − u)/t is the rate of change of velocity, in m s⁻².
Example: a car goes from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 s. a = (30 − 10)/5 = 4 m s⁻².

On a displacement-time graph, gradient = velocity. On a velocity-time graph, gradient = acceleration and area under the graph = displacement. A horizontal line on a velocity-time graph means uniform velocity.
All objects in free fall accelerate at g ≈ 9.81 m s⁻² when air resistance is ignored, whatever their mass. In a vacuum, a feather and a coin fall together.
Example: a stone falls for 2 s. v = gt = 9.81 × 2 = 19.6 m/s.

Inertia is an object's tendency to stay at rest or keep moving uniformly (Newton's First Law). The larger the mass, the greater the inertia. Seat belts and airbags protect passengers from inertia when a car stops suddenly.

Malaysia: the TRIGA PUSPATI research reactor.

nota.t: Nuclear energy is used to generate electricity, in medicine (radiotherapy, sterilising instruments, imaging), agriculture (new crop varieties, preserving food with gamma rays), industry (thickness gauges, leak detection) and archaeology (carbon-14 dating).

Nuclear energy comes from nuclear fission (a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 is hit by a neutron and splits, releasing more neutrons and energy in a chain reaction) or nuclear fusion (light nuclei join, as in the Sun). The energy is E = mc², where m is the mass defect.
Example: mass defect 1 × 10⁻²⁸ kg → E = 1 × 10⁻²⁸ × (3 × 10⁸)² = 9 × 10⁻¹² J.

Benefits of nuclear energy: lots of energy from little fuel and no CO₂ released during generation. Drawbacks: long-lasting radioactive waste, accident risk (Chernobyl 1986, Fukushima 2011) and high cost. Ionising radiation can cause cancer and mutations; warning signs and dose monitoring are needed.

In Malaysia, the Malaysian Nuclear Agency runs the TRIGA PUSPATI research reactor in Bangi (since 1982) for research, medicine and industry. The Atomic Energy Licensing Board (AELB) regulates radiation safety under the Atomic Energy Licensing Act 1984.
